newsitem.title: USA: Tame March US CPI allays market fears, bonds rally.
newsitem.headline: Tame March US CPI allays market fears, bonds rally.

text.p: The U.S. March consumer price index (CPI) allayed market fears of an acceleration in price growth, sparking a rally in U.S. debt markets and easing the pressure on Federal Reserve policymakers to raise interest rates, experts said on Tuesday.
"It doesn't live up to investors' worst fears which is why the market is getting a nice little bounce off it," said Kevin Flanagan, an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"We have no major acceleration in inflation, but that didn't stop the Fed from tightening back in March," he added.

While the 0.1 percent rise in March CPI was below market expectations for a 0.2 percent rise and February's 0.3 percent gain, Fed policymakers need to see a slowing in consumer demand or overall economic growth before backing down from their current tightening stance, economists said.
"I think this number does not force the Fed to have to change policy right away," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G Edwards & Sons Inc.
"It might allow the Fed to hold policy steady if we continue to see good inflation news like this," he added.
The central bank raised the federal funds rate target 25 basis points to 5.5 percent on March 25, the first official U.S. rate rise in more than two years.

In a Reuter poll taken March 26, 15 out of 31 experts expected the Fed to lift the federal funds rate an additional 25 basis points at its next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on May 20. By early June, 23 out of 28 pundits said the target would hit at least 5.75 percent.
"For the Fed, it still has to be forward looking and the overall economy still has ample forward momentum. This is old news," said money market economist Raphael Marrone.
"It doesn't detract at all from the hike they initiated last month," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Marrone added.
U.S. Treasuries rallied on the news. The 30-year long bond jumped more than a point in a knee-jerk reaction and held on to most of its gains, settling up 27/32 at 94-05/32 to yield 7.10 percent.
Equities also were boosted by the report. The Dow Jones Industrials index opened up 10 points and had climbed over 80 points by 0940 EDT/1340 GMT.
Meanwhile, the dollar temporarily dipped against the mark and yen, but quickly recovered back to its opening levels.

Regarding the components of the Labor Department's CPI report, an unanticipated drop in apparel prices and no growth in housing prices caused the overall index to fall short of expectations, economists said.
"The internals of this number are just really, really good. The apparel and housing numbers were a lot better than expected," said Joe Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Apparel and upkeep prices fell 0.3 percent after rising 0.2 percent in February while housing prices were unchanged following a 0.3 percent rise in the prior month.
The core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, also underperformed market expectations, rising 0.2 percent compared to an anticipated 0.3 percent rise.
